title: Ideology and the Map: Toward a Postmodern Visual Design Practice
author: Ben F. Barton
Marthalee S. Barton
citation: Barton, B. F., & Barton, M. S. (1993a). Ideology and the map: Toward a postmodern visual design practice. In N. R. Blyler & C. Thralls (Eds.), Professional communication: The social perspective (pp. 49–78). Sage.
annotation: Barton and Barton read maps as ideological documents. A map looks natural because its rules of inclusion and exclusion stay out of view, and those rules decide whose world gets drawn. The chapter is the field's standard starting point for critical work on technical visuals, and it gives you a vocabulary for what a chart leaves out.
ucf: Print reprint in Central Works in Technical Communication (2004), chapter 16, call number T11 .C43 2004. The original Sage volume needs interlibrary loan.

title: Modes of Power in Technical and Professional Visuals
author: Ben F. Barton
Marthalee S. Barton
publisher: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
citation: Barton, B. F., & Barton, M. S. (1993b). Modes of power in technical and professional visuals. Journal of Business and Technical Communication, 7(1), 138–162. https://doi.org/10.1177/1050651993007001007
annotation: This article applies Foucault's account of surveillance to tables, charts, and diagrams. Synoptic visuals let a viewer take in a whole population at a glance, and analytic visuals divide and rank what they show. It belongs here because it treats the data display as an instrument of institutional power, and Hartzog (2025) in Section 3 still uses its terms.

title: Cruel Pies: The Inhumanity of Technical Illustrations
author: Sam Dragga
Dan Voss
citation: Dragga, S., & Voss, D. (2001). Cruel pies: The inhumanity of technical illustrations. Technical Communication, 48(3), 265–274.
annotation: Dragga and Voss argue that conventional charts of deaths and injuries are ethically incomplete because they strip out the people the numbers count. They propose adding pictorial and human elements to statistical graphics. The article started the field's conversation about humanizing data, which Kostelnick (2016) in Section 2 continues.

title: Gender, Technology, and the History of Technical Communication
author: Katherine T. Durack
citation: Durack, K. T. (1997). Gender, technology, and the history of technical communication. Technical Communication Quarterly, 6(3), 249–260. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq0603_2
annotation: Durack asks why women are missing from histories of technical communication. Her answer is that the field's working definitions of technology, work, and workplace exclude the household and the kinds of writing women did. The article shows that a definition can erase a group before any document is written, which is the logic your dissertation tracks in federal data.

title: Theory of Visual Rhetoric
author: Sonja K. Foss
citation: Foss, S. K. (2005). Theory of visual rhetoric. In K. Smith, S. Moriarty, G. Barbatsis, & K. Kenney (Eds.), Handbook of visual communication: Theory, methods, and media (pp. 141–152). Lawrence Erlbaum.
annotation: Foss defines visual rhetoric in two senses: a visual object that communicates, and a way of studying such objects. She sets out what a rhetorical analysis of an image should attend to, namely its nature, its function, and how well it performs that function. It is the standard short statement from rhetorical studies, and it balances the list's technical communication sources.
ucf: Print copy at the Main Library, call number P93.5 .H36. A scan of the chapter is in the Drive folder.

title: The Ethic of Expediency: Classical Rhetoric, Technology, and the Holocaust
author: Steven B. Katz
citation: Katz, S. B. (1992). The ethic of expediency: Classical rhetoric, technology, and the Holocaust. College English, 54(3), 255–275. https://doi.org/10.58680/ce19929392
annotation: Katz analyzes a Nazi memo about modifying gas vans and finds it a well-made technical document by textbook standards. He argues that Western technical writing runs on an ethic of expediency in which efficiency becomes its own justification. It is the field's central text on ethics and the clearest case that a technical document's style has moral content.

title: The Rhetoric of Neutrality
author: Robin Kinross
citation: Kinross, R. (1985). The rhetoric of neutrality. Design Issues, 2(2), 18–30. https://doi.org/10.2307/1511415
annotation: Kinross takes a railway timetable, the kind of document designers offer as pure information, and shows the persuasive choices in its type and layout. He argues that the modernist claim to neutral information design is itself a rhetorical stance with a history. It is the design studies source for the idea that information design always involves rhetoric.

title: An Approach for Applying Cultural Study Theory to Technical Writing Research
author: Bernadette Longo
citation: Longo, B. (1998). An approach for applying cultural study theory to technical writing research. Technical Communication Quarterly, 7(1), 53–73. https://doi.org/10.1080/10572259809364617
annotation: Longo argues that studies of single workplaces cannot explain why technical writing takes the forms it does. She proposes a cultural studies approach, drawing on Foucault, that treats technical writing as a practice that legitimates some knowledge and devalues other knowledge. It opened the cultural critique that later became the social justice turn.

title: A Humanistic Rationale for Technical Writing
author: Carolyn R. Miller
citation: Miller, C. R. (1979). A humanistic rationale for technical writing. College English, 40(6), 610–617. https://doi.org/10.58680/ce197916058
annotation: Miller argues that technical writing is taught as a neutral skill because it inherits a positivist view of science, in which language is a clear window onto facts. She proposes a rhetorical view in which technical writing is participation in a community's way of knowing. Nearly every later argument about the rhetoric of technical communication starts from this essay.

title: Genre as Social Action
author: Carolyn R. Miller
citation: Miller, C. R. (1984). Genre as social action. Quarterly Journal of Speech, 70(2), 151–167. https://doi.org/10.1080/00335638409383686
annotation: Miller defines a genre as a typified action that responds to a recurring social situation. Learning a genre therefore means learning what ends a community lets its members pursue. The article is the base of rhetorical genre studies, and it is what allows a form or a report to be read as an action.

title: Sense and Sensibility in Technical Documentation: How Feminist Interpretation Strategies Can Save Lives in the Nation's Mines
author: Beverly A. Sauer
publisher: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
citation: Sauer, B. A. (1993). Sense and sensibility in technical documentation: How feminist interpretation strategies can save lives in the nation's mines. Journal of Business and Technical Communication, 7(1), 63–83. https://doi.org/10.1177/1050651993007001004
annotation: Sauer reads federal mine accident reports through feminist theory. She shows that the reports' conventions exclude the embodied, local knowledge of miners and their families, and that the exclusion has consequences for safety. It is an early model of the analysis you do: a close reading of what an official document's form leaves no room to say.

title: The Politics of the Interface: Power and Its Exercise in Electronic Contact Zones
author: Cynthia L. Selfe
Richard J. Selfe, Jr.
citation: Selfe, C. L., & Selfe, R. J., Jr. (1994). The politics of the interface: Power and its exercise in electronic contact zones. College Composition and Communication, 45(4), 480–504. https://doi.org/10.58680/ccc19948766
annotation: Selfe and Selfe read the computer desktop as a map of cultural assumptions. Its metaphors and defaults favor white, middle-class, English-speaking, corporate users and treat other users as exceptions. The article connects the two sides of this area because it reads an interface as both a technical document and a visual argument.

title: The Technical Communicator as Author: Meaning, Power, Authority
author: Jennifer Daryl Slack
David James Miller
Jeffrey Doak
publisher: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
citation: Slack, J. D., Miller, D. J., & Doak, J. (1993). The technical communicator as author: Meaning, power, authority. Journal of Business and Technical Communication, 7(1), 12–36. https://doi.org/10.1177/1050651993007001002
annotation: The authors compare three views of communication: transmission, translation, and articulation. Under the articulation view, technical communicators take part in making meaning and in the power relations a document carries, so they bear an author's responsibility. The article is the standard source for rejecting the idea of the technical communicator as a neutral conduit.

title: "Missing/Unspecified": Demographic Data Visualization During the COVID-19 Pandemic
author: Rachel Atherton
publisher: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
citation: Atherton, R. (2021). "Missing/unspecified": Demographic data visualization during the COVID-19 pandemic. Journal of Business and Technical Communication, 35(1), 80–87. https://doi.org/10.1177/1050651920957982
annotation: Atherton shows that early CDC data on COVID-19 listed race as "missing/unspecified" at high rates, and that public visualizations did not reflect what the datasets lacked. She argues that incomplete demographic data hides the pandemic's effect on marginalized communities. It is short, and it is the piece on this list closest to your CDC material.

title: Florence Nightingale's Visual Rhetoric in the Rose Diagrams
author: Lee Brasseur
citation: Brasseur, L. (2005). Florence Nightingale's visual rhetoric in the rose diagrams. Technical Communication Quarterly, 14(2), 161–182. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1402_3
annotation: Brasseur analyzes the rose diagrams Florence Nightingale designed to show causes of death in the Crimean War. She shows how the sequence and form of the diagrams were built to move government readers toward sanitary reform. It is the field's model historical study of a statistical graphic made to persuade.

title: Humanities Approaches to Graphical Display
author: Johanna Drucker
citation: Drucker, J. (2011). Humanities approaches to graphical display. Digital Humanities Quarterly, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.63744/r4ysrh7ae534
annotation: Drucker argues that charts borrowed from the sciences present data as given when all data are taken and constructed, and she proposes the term "capta." One of her examples is a bar chart of men and women by nation, which she uses to show how a chart fixes gender as a binary and nations as stable units. It comes from digital humanities, and it is the strongest theoretical statement on this list that a visualization is an interpretation.
ucf: Catalog record · open access at DHQ

title: Apparent Feminism as a Methodology for Technical Communication and Rhetoric
author: Erin A. Frost
publisher: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
citation: Frost, E. A. (2016). Apparent feminism as a methodology for technical communication and rhetoric. Journal of Business and Technical Communication, 30(1), 3–28. https://doi.org/10.1177/1050651915602295
annotation: Frost proposes apparent feminism, a methodology that makes the need for feminist critique visible in settings that present themselves as neutral. It asks researchers to question claims of efficiency and objectivity and to count more people as audiences. It gives you a named method from inside the field for reading supposedly neutral technical documents.

title: Race, Rhetoric, and Technology: A Case Study of Decolonial Technical Communication Theory, Methodology, and Pedagogy
author: Angela M. Haas
publisher: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
citation: Haas, A. M. (2012). Race, rhetoric, and technology: A case study of decolonial technical communication theory, methodology, and pedagogy. Journal of Business and Technical Communication, 26(3), 277–310. https://doi.org/10.1177/1050651912439539
annotation: Haas reports on a graduate course built around race, rhetoric, and technology and uses it to set out a decolonial approach to technical communication. She argues that race, rhetoric, and technology shape one another and should be studied together. Later social justice scholarship in the field cites this article as a starting point.

title: Visualization Rhetoric: Framing Effects in Narrative Visualization
author: Jessica Hullman
Nicholas Diakopoulos
publisher: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
citation: Hullman, J., & Diakopoulos, N. (2011). Visualization rhetoric: Framing effects in narrative visualization. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 17(12), 2231–2240. https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2011.255
annotation: The authors analyze narrative visualizations and identify the techniques designers use to steer interpretation, such as omission, emphasis, and annotation. They organize these techniques by the layer where they operate, from the data to the interactivity. The article comes from visualization research, and it is the source of "visualization rhetoric" as a term.

title: Disrupting the Past to Disrupt the Future: An Antenarrative of Technical Communication
author: Natasha N. Jones
Kristen R. Moore
Rebecca Walton
citation: Jones, N. N., Moore, K. R., & Walton, R. (2016). Disrupting the past to disrupt the future: An antenarrative of technical communication. Technical Communication Quarterly, 25(4), 211–229. https://doi.org/10.1080/10572252.2016.1224655
annotation: The authors argue that the field's dominant story about itself, centered on efficiency and pragmatism, has hidden a long line of work on inclusion. They reweave that history as an antenarrative and introduce positionality, privilege, and power as terms for analysis. The article stands in here for the social justice turn, since the 2019 book is on your core list.

title: Technologies of Disenfranchisement: Literacy Tests and Black Voters in the US from 1890 to 1965
author: Natasha N. Jones
Miriam F. Williams
citation: Jones, N. N., & Williams, M. F. (2018). Technologies of disenfranchisement: Literacy tests and Black voters in the US from 1890 to 1965. Technical Communication, 65(4), 371–386.
annotation: Jones and Williams read the literacy tests used to block Black voters from 1890 to 1965 as technical documents. They show that the tests' design, instructions, and administration were built to produce failure. It models your kind of argument: an official form treated as a technology that sorts people.

title: The Work That Visualisation Conventions Do
author: Helen Kennedy
Rosemary Lucy Hill
Giorgia Aiello
William Allen
citation: Kennedy, H., Hill, R. L., Aiello, G., & Allen, W. (2016). The work that visualisation conventions do. Information, Communication & Society, 19(6), 715–735. https://doi.org/10.1080/1369118X.2016.1153126
annotation: The authors identify four conventions of data visualization: two-dimensional viewpoints, clean layouts, geometric shapes and lines, and the inclusion of data sources. They argue that these conventions make a visualization look objective and so do persuasive work. It comes from critical data studies and extends the account of conventions in Kostelnick and Hassett (2003) to contemporary data graphics.

title: London Through Rose-Colored Graphics: Visual Rhetoric and Information Graphic Design in Charles Booth's Maps of London Poverty
author: Miles A. Kimball
publisher: Journal of Technical Writing and Communication
citation: Kimball, M. A. (2006). London through rose-colored graphics: Visual rhetoric and information graphic design in Charles Booth's maps of London poverty. Journal of Technical Writing and Communication, 36(4), 353–381. https://doi.org/10.2190/K561-40P2-5422-PTG2
annotation: Kimball studies the color-coded poverty maps Charles Booth made of London in the late nineteenth century. He argues that the maps turned a classification of social classes into a clear and reassuring picture, and that this appeal to order helps explain their influence. It pairs a classification scheme with its visualization, which is the combination you study.

title: The Visual Rhetoric of Data Displays: The Conundrum of Clarity
author: Charles Kostelnick
citation: Kostelnick, C. (2008). The visual rhetoric of data displays: The conundrum of clarity. IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication, 51(1), 116–130. https://doi.org/10.1109/TPC.2007.914869
annotation: Kostelnick reviews how clarity in charts and graphs has been defined, from perceptual rules to rhetorical judgment. He argues that clarity depends on audience, purpose, and the conventions readers know, so no display is clear in itself. The article first ran in December 2007 (volume 50, issue 4, pp. 280–294) and was reprinted in March 2008, and this entry cites the reprint.

title: The Re-Emergence of Emotional Appeals in Interactive Data Visualization
author: Charles Kostelnick
citation: Kostelnick, C. (2016). The re-emergence of emotional appeals in interactive data visualization. Technical Communication, 63(2), 116–135.
annotation: Kostelnick traces emotional appeals in data design from their presence in earlier graphics, through their suppression under modernist minimalism, to their return in interactive visualization. He shows how interactive displays invite readers to feel as well as compare. It updates the humanizing argument of Dragga and Voss (2001) for digital displays.

title: Data Our Bodies Tell: Towards Critical Feminist Action in Fertility and Period Tracking Applications
author: Maria Novotny
Les Hutchinson
citation: Novotny, M., & Hutchinson, L. (2019). Data our bodies tell: Towards critical feminist action in fertility and period tracking applications. Technical Communication Quarterly, 28(4), 332–360. https://doi.org/10.1080/10572252.2019.1607907
annotation: Novotny and Hutchinson analyze fertility and period tracking apps as technical communication. They show how the apps collect and use intimate body data and argue for a critical feminist approach to their design and use. It is the field's main article on body data and interfaces.

title: Forms as Boundary Genres in Medicine, Science, and Business
author: Susan L. Popham
publisher: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
citation: Popham, S. L. (2005). Forms as boundary genres in medicine, science, and business. Journal of Business and Technical Communication, 19(3), 279–303. https://doi.org/10.1177/1050651905275624
annotation: Popham studies the forms that move between a medical practice, its insurers, and its business office. She argues that forms act as boundary genres that carry one profession's values into another's work. It is the most direct treatment of forms in the field's journals.

title: Mapping the Research Questions in Technical Communication
author: Carolyn D. Rude
publisher: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
citation: Rude, C. D. (2009). Mapping the research questions in technical communication. Journal of Business and Technical Communication, 23(2), 174–215. https://doi.org/10.1177/1050651908329562
annotation: Rude reviews the field's scholarship and proposes that one question unites it: how texts and related practices mediate knowledge, values, and action in social and professional settings. She groups research into four areas: disciplinarity, pedagogy, practice, and social change. It is the reference point for claims about what the field studies.

title: Designing Outrage, Programming Discord: A Critical Interface Analysis of Facebook as a Campaign Technology
author: Jennifer Sano-Franchini
citation: Sano-Franchini, J. (2018). Designing outrage, programming discord: A critical interface analysis of Facebook as a campaign technology. Technical Communication, 65(4), 387–410.
annotation: Sano-Franchini introduces critical interface analysis and applies it to Facebook as a campaign technology. She shows how the interface's design choices encourage outrage and discord. Chen, Pandey, and Baniya (2025) in Section 3 use her method.

title: The Interface as Discourse: The Production of Norms Through Web Design
author: Mel Stanfill
citation: Stanfill, M. (2015). The interface as discourse: The production of norms through web design. New Media & Society, 17(7), 1059–1074. https://doi.org/10.1177/1461444814520873
annotation: Stanfill proposes discursive interface analysis, which reads a site's features, layout, and defaults for what they assume users are and should do. Interfaces produce norms by making some uses easy and others hard. It comes from media studies, and it gives a clear method for reading an interface as a document.

title: Toward Data Justice: Understanding Police Shooting Data Systems and Narratives
author: Rachel Atherton
citation: Atherton, R. (2022). Toward data justice: Understanding police shooting data systems and narratives. IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication, 65(1), 118–134. https://doi.org/10.1109/TPC.2021.3138008
annotation: Atherton studies the Washington Post's Fatal Force database, which was created in 2015 to fill a gap in official data on police use of force. She examines how choices about collecting, aggregating, and curating records shape the stories the data can tell. It is the closest match on this list to your counter-data strand.
studyType: Case study of a data system, using narrative methods.
rhetoricalConcept: Data system design as rhetorical, read through narrative and data justice.

title: Navigating Immigration as an Alien: A Critical Interface Analysis of the US Citizenship and Immigration Services Website
author: Jianfen Chen
Shyam Pandey
Sweta Baniya
citation: Chen, J., Pandey, S., & Baniya, S. (2025). Navigating immigration as an alien: A critical interface analysis of the US Citizenship and Immigration Services website. IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication, 68(1), 22–40. https://doi.org/10.1109/TPC.2025.3528758
annotation: The authors analyze the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services website to show how a government site builds systemic barriers into its design for minoritized and multilingual users. They assess its content against accessibility guidelines and from the user's side. It extends interface critique to a federal agency's public documents.
rhetoricalConcept: The interface as a site of power, following Sano-Franchini (2018), joined to linguistic social justice.

title: "It Must Be a System Thing": Information Infrastructure Genres as Sites of Inequity
author: Dana Comi
citation: Comi, D. (2022). "It must be a system thing": Information infrastructure genres as sites of inequity. Communication Design Quarterly, 10(3), 22–32. https://doi.org/10.1145/3507870.3507874
annotation: Comi interviews participants in the WIC nutrition program and focuses on the Approved Product List, the document that tells participants what they may buy. She shows that the list standardizes benefit redemption in ways that make participants more visible and more vulnerable. It demonstrates how to locate inequity in one mundane federal document.
rhetoricalConcept: Genre, applied to the documents that make up a federal information infrastructure.

title: Charting a New Course: An Inventory of Data Visualization Scholarship in TPC From 2013 to 2023
author: Sara C. Doan
Steven S. Brooks
citation: Doan, S. C., & Brooks, S. S. (2026). Charting a new course: An inventory of data visualization scholarship in TPC from 2013 to 2023. IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication, 69(2), 168–182. https://doi.org/10.1109/TPC.2026.3686896
annotation: Doan and Brooks review the data visualization scholarship published in the field from 2013 to 2023. They sort it by the kinds of articles published, the cases studied, and the disciplines scholars draw from. It is here as a map of the conversation that the other visual studies in this section join.
rhetoricalConcept: None applied to a case; the article categorizes how the field studies visualization.

title: Trans and Queer Visibility in an Era of Hyper Surveillance: A User Experience Study of University Systems for Sharing Gender Pronouns
author: McKinley Green
publisher: Journal of Technical Writing and Communication
citation: Green, M. (2026). Trans and queer visibility in an era of hyper surveillance: A user experience study of university systems for sharing gender pronouns. Journal of Technical Writing and Communication, 56(1), 35–60. https://doi.org/10.1177/00472816251384913
annotation: Green studies how college students use university systems for sharing a chosen name and pronouns. The systems promise inclusion, and they also make gender nonconformity visible to institutions at a time when pronouns are a target of government and board policy. It is the most direct recent study of how a data field for gender exposes the people who fill it in.
rhetoricalConcept: Visibility, drawn from trans and queer scholarship and applied to design.

title: 'Flatten the Curve': Rhetorical Data Visualizations of a Global Pandemic
author: Molly Hartzog
citation: Hartzog, M. (2025). 'Flatten the curve': Rhetorical data visualizations of a global pandemic. Technical Communication Quarterly, 34(1), 114–129. https://doi.org/10.1080/10572252.2024.2374379
annotation: Hartzog analyzes "flatten the curve" graphics and COVID-19 dashboards to ask when a metric persuades people to act. She finds that actionable metrics persuade when they connect one person's behavior to the whole outbreak. It shows two Section 1 frameworks still at work in current analysis.
rhetoricalConcept: Modes of power (Barton & Barton, 1993b) and visual conventions (Kostelnick & Hassett, 2003).

title: Archives, Rhetorical Absence, and Critical Imagination: Examining Black Women's Mental Health Narratives at Virginia's Central State Hospital
author: Natasha N. Jones
Miriam F. Williams
citation: Jones, N. N., & Williams, M. F. (2022). Archives, rhetorical absence, and critical imagination: Examining Black women's mental health narratives at Virginia's Central State Hospital. IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication, 65(1), 179–196. https://doi.org/10.1109/TPC.2022.3140883
annotation: Jones and Williams examine annual reports from Virginia's Central State Hospital from the late 1800s and early 1900s. They show how the reports characterize Black women patients or leave them out, and they treat those absences as evidence. It gives you a method for reading what an institutional record omits.
rhetoricalConcept: Rhetorical absence, paired with critical imagination.

title: Defining the Racial and Ethnic "Other": Constructing an American Identity Through Visualizing Census Data in the U.S. Statistical Atlases
author: Li Li
publisher: Journal of Technical Writing and Communication
citation: Li, L. (2022). Defining the racial and ethnic "other": Constructing an American identity through visualizing census data in the U.S. Statistical Atlases. Journal of Technical Writing and Communication, 52(4), 460–492. https://doi.org/10.1177/00472816221086523
annotation: Li analyzes how the U.S. Statistical Atlases from 1874 to 1925 visualized census data on immigrants and African Americans. The charts and maps defined a "native white" population against racial and ethnic others and set a hierarchy among them. It is the nearest precedent for studying how federal data graphics construct identity categories.
rhetoricalConcept: A framework for how data design marginalizes racial and ethnic minority groups.

title: A Stasis Network Methodology to Reckon with the Rhetorical Process of Data: How a Data Team Qualified Meaning and Practices
author: Chris A. Lindgren
citation: Lindgren, C. A. (2024). A stasis network methodology to reckon with the rhetorical process of data: How a data team qualified meaning and practices. Technical Communication Quarterly, 33(4), 475–500. https://doi.org/10.1080/10572252.2024.2306259
annotation: Lindgren studies a data journalism team as it prepares a report and maps where members confronted competing definitions of metrics. Those definitions shaped what the team treated as significant and as ethically possible. It shows that the meaning of a number is argued out before any chart is drawn.
studyType: Qualitative study of a data team.
rhetoricalConcept: Stasis, extended into a network method.

title: User Perceptions of Actionability in Data Dashboards
author: Madeleine Sorapure
publisher: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
citation: Sorapure, M. (2023). User perceptions of actionability in data dashboards. Journal of Business and Technical Communication, 37(3), 253–280. https://doi.org/10.1177/10506519231161611
annotation: Sorapure observes nonexpert users working with COVID-19 dashboards and asks whether the dashboards help them decide what to do. She finds that users want data at personal and local scales and that emotional response matters to use. It supplies user evidence for claims the Section 2 sources make from design analysis.
studyType: Multiphase user study with recorded interviews.
rhetoricalConcept: Actionability, an audience-centered measure of whether a display supports decisions.

title: Precarious Data: Crack, Opioids, and Enacting a Social Justice Ethic in Data Visualization Practice
author: Candice A. Welhausen
citation: Welhausen, C. A. (2022). Precarious data: Crack, opioids, and enacting a social justice ethic in data visualization practice. IEEE Transactions on Professional Communication, 65(1), 50–69. https://doi.org/10.1109/TPC.2022.3144826
annotation: Welhausen examines the data visualizations in media reporting on crack cocaine and on opioids. She asks how the visuals position drug use as a criminal justice problem or as a public health issue, and she proposes a social justice ethic for visualization practice. It applies framing analysis, usually done on language, to charts.
studyType: Analysis of data visualizations in news coverage.

title: Please Provide the Following Information: Enthymemes and the Logics of Individual Responsibility in the Patient Medical History Form
author: Kelly A. Whitney
citation: Whitney, K. A. (2025). Please provide the following information: Enthymemes and the logics of individual responsibility in the patient medical history form. Technical Communication Quarterly, 34(1), 1–23. https://doi.org/10.1080/10572252.2023.2299465
annotation: Whitney analyzes patient medical history forms from different periods and settings. She finds that the forms teach patients to see health as a matter of genetics and personal choice, an assumption the forms never state. It is the closest recent model for a rhetorical analysis of a form.
rhetoricalConcept: The enthymeme, used to show how a form's questions carry unstated premises.
